newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain promises "fresh start" with EU partners.
newsitem.headline: Britain promises "fresh start" with EU partners.

text.p: - Britain's new Labour government promised a "fresh start" with the European Union on Monday, pledging to work with, rather than fight, its EU partners.

"We want to work with you as colleagues in a shared enterprise...not using the language of opponents," Doug Henderson, Labour's new Europe minister, told representatives of EU states meeting to negotiate a new EU treaty.
"Europe, for the new British government, is an opportunity, not a threat."
In the first meeting between a new British minister and EU partners, Henderson said Britain wanted to make the Union more democratic, more open and more relevant to ordinary people.

In sharp contrast to the ousted Conservatives, Henderson said Labour would end the British opt-out from the EU's Social Chapter, agree to more qualified majority voting in some policy areas and support an employment chapter in a new EU treaty to be adopted in mid-June in Amsterdam.
He also hinted at a more flexible British approach to areas of foreign policy and justice and home affairs.
But Henderson made clear Britain would maintain its border controls and said he hoped EU partners would show understanding in a number of areas in which Britain has concerns.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook earlier heralded a more cooperative British presence in Europe following 18 years of Conservative rule during which Britain has often isolated itself from the rest of Europe.

"I'm in favour of getting the best deal for Britain and we very strongly believe we will get a better deal...if we work together with the other states of Europe, not constantly fight them," he told Sky Television.
"We won't allow ourselves to be bounced and we're not going to be sold out."

Henderson's key message was that Labour was committed to joining the Social Chapter, set up to regulate working conditions across Europe. The Conservatives had consistently opposed social plans which, they said, would cost 500,000 jobs.

Cook, insisting that British workers should enjoy the same rights as their EU counterparts, said there was nothing to fear in the Social Chapter and added that many big firms already followed its guidelines.
"We are committed to achieving a skilled, flexible workforce. And the key to a competitive Britain is to make sure we have that committed workforce," he said.
But there remain some sceptical voices in business.
Adair Turner, head of the influential Confederation of British Industry, urged Britain not to ape the "mistaken" labour policies of some EU members and thereby damage job creation.
"The concern has always been...not what is in it at the moment, but where it could lead to in time if it is used in a mistaken fashion," he told BBC radio.
Lord Howe, former Conservative foreign minister and a leading pro-European, welcomed Labour's attempt to patch up relations with Brussels.
"The arrival of new people with a new tone of voice will make it easier to sell good British points, which ought to be sold well," he said, echoing Labour's own message.
The incoming government is keen to show the EU a friendlier face than the Conservatives and says it is easier to chalk up victories through negotiation than via confrontation.
Cook has pledged that he will give a higher profile to the environment and human rights, and will send ministers, rather than civil servants, to all talks on EU integration.

However, Labour intends to retain Britain's veto on social security issues, keep control over external borders and doubts that Britain would join up to the planned single currency in the first membership wave of 1999.
